key_facts: **Dermatofibroma** (benign fibrous histiocytoma) is a common firm dermal papule, usually on the **legs**.
Firm 'button' with a brown rim; the **dimple sign**: it puckers inwards when pinched.
Dermoscopy: central white scar-like patch with a fine peripheral pigment network.
Benign: reassure. Refer if growing, large, atypical or pigmented in an unusual way (exclude melanoma and DFSP).
Excision leaves a scar often worse than the lesion.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Dermatofibroma (DF) is a very common benign fibrohistiocytic proliferation in the dermis. It is seen mostly in adults aged 20–50 and is more common in women. It is a reactive or neoplastic nodule; which of the two is still debated.

A dermatofibroma (core: the [skin lumps](condition:dermatofibroma) notes) with marked overlying epidermal hyperpigmentation. It is **commoner and darker in skin of colour**, so it is often brought in as a "mole".

sub: Young to middle-aged adults, more women; lower legs commonest.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors

ul: Often follows minor trauma such as an insect bite, folliculitis or a shaving nick, but many patients recall none.
Dermal fibroblasts and histiocytes proliferate and trap collagen bundles at the periphery. The overlying epidermis is induced to thicken and hyperpigment, which is why the surface is often brown.
Multiple (eruptive) DFs (≥15, or many appearing quickly) are associated with altered immunity: SLE, HIV, immunosuppressive drugs and pregnancy.
Histology: Factor XIIIa positive, CD34 negative. This is the reverse of DFSP (see *Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans*), and the stain pair is a favourite exam question.

blocks: Dermal fibrohistiocytic proliferation induces the overlying epidermis to thicken (acanthosis) and to increase basal melanin ("dirty fingers" rete ridges). Haemosiderin deposits make the aneurysmal/haemosiderotic variant blue-black.

ul: Possibly a reaction to minor trauma such as an insect bite or ingrown hair; multiple lesions in immunosuppression (HIV, lupus).
**"It's a mole"**: it is a fibrous lesion, which explains its firmness and the dimple sign.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A dermatofibroma is a **fibrous reaction** in the dermis that tethers the skin above.

mech.t: Minor trauma triggers fibroblasts and histiocytes to proliferate in the dermis.
Collagen and cells form a firm nodule that tethers the overlying epidermis.
mech.caption: The dimple sign: pinching pushes the dermatofibroma downwards.

mech.t: Overlying epidermis thickens and becomes pigmented, causing the brown rim.

histo: Spindle cells and histiocytes trapping collagen bundles at the periphery ('collagen balls'); overlying acanthosis with basal pigmentation; CD34 negative (unlike DFSP).

ul: Firm to hard papule or nodule, 3–10 mm, that feels like a "button" tethered to the skin but mobile over deeper tissue.
Colour varies (skin-coloured, pink, brown, or a darker rim with a paler centre), especially in darker skin (see the [benign lesion](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis) notes, pigmented DF).
**Lower legs** are the classic site, then arms and trunk. Usually solitary and asymptomatic. It may itch or be tender, and it is often nicked when shaving.
**Dimple (Fitzpatrick / pinch) sign:** pinching the lesion from the sides makes it dimple inward.

Variants to know: cellular, aneurysmal/haemosiderotic (can enlarge quickly and look blue-black), atypical ("pseudosarcomatous"), and deep or subcutaneous. **Cellular, aneurysmal and atypical variants recur more often after excision, and rare cases metastasise.** This is the course [Case 1](condition:dermatofibroma) answer.
A firm 3–10 mm papule, brown to dark brown, often **darker at the rim with a paler centre**. Sometimes pink-brown.
Limbs (arms in [Case 1](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis), legs classically). Slow growth over years. A positive dimple sign.

sub: A slowly enlarging firm plaque over 2–3 cm, especially on the trunk, may be dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans: refer.

ul: Clinical: typical site, firmness, and the dimple sign.
Dermoscopy: a delicate peripheral pigment network with a **central white scar-like patch**. The commonest pattern, but not universal.
Biopsy is needed only for atypical lesions: >1 cm, rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, recurrence after removal, unusual site (face, scalp, acral), or doubt between DF and a melanocytic lesion.

Pinch test. Dermoscopy: **delicate peripheral pigment network + central white scar-like area**. Some show a bland structureless or homogeneous pattern, and those are less reassuring, so refer if unsure.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Melanocytic naevus; **melanoma** (EFG, change, irregular dermoscopy); pigmented BCC (pearly, ovoid nests, arborising vessels); SK (stuck-on, milia-like cysts); post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation over a prurigo nodule; blue naevus.

ul: **Typical DF:** reassure and give the BAD/DermNet leaflet. **No biopsy or removal is needed.- **Removal for cosmetic reasons only is generally not funded on the NHS.** NHS England's *Evidence-Based Interventions* programme and local "procedures of limited clinical value" policies restrict benign lesion removal to set criteria: diagnostic doubt, recurrent bleeding/infection, functional impairment or significant pain. Excision leaves a scar often larger and more visible than the DF, and incomplete removal (DF extends deeper than it looks) leads to recurrence.
Cryotherapy or shave can flatten a DF but often leaves a white mark and recurrence. These are specialist or GP-surgeon decisions, not IP.
**Refer (routine dermatology)** if diagnosis is uncertain, a variant is suspected, or the lesion is >1 cm and growing.

**Refer urgently** (two-week-wait / suspected cancer pathway) if it may be melanoma: NG12 weighted 7-point checklist ≥3, or features of nodular melanoma. Refer urgently (sarcoma or dermatology as per local pathway) if DFSP is suspected (see *Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans*).
Classic DF features plus the dimple sign: reassure; leaflet.

**Any doubt about a melanocytic lesion in darker skin: refer** (routine dermatology/teledermatology with dermoscopic). If the 7-point score is ≥3 (e.g. change in size + irregular colour), use the **suspected cancer pathway**.
Removal on cosmetic grounds is not routinely NHS-funded (the [skin lumps](condition:dermatofibroma) notes see *Pigmented dermatofibroma*).

blocks.h: Case 1: 42-year-old woman, firm dome-shaped skin-coloured papule on the leg for 8 months

ul: **Diagnosis:** dermatofibroma.
**Bedside test:** dimple (pinch/Fitzpatrick) sign. Dermoscopy: peripheral network with a central white patch.
**Subtype with recurrence/metastatic potential:** cellular (also aneurysmal and atypical) fibrous histiocytoma.

**Management (UK teaching answer):** reassure; no biopsy or removal for a typical lesion. Removal only for symptoms or diagnostic doubt, within local funding criteria. Refer if atypical (>1 cm, growing, ulcerated, recurrent) or if the 7-point checklist is ≥3. The course "excise with a 3–5 mm margin" is a reasonable specialist approach *if* excision is indicated, not a routine plan (see *Where course teaching differs from UK guidance*).

blocks.h: Case 2: 5-year-old boy, congenital hairless scalp patch, now thicker and yellow-orange

ul: **Diagnosis:** sebaceous naevus of Jadassohn (pubertal/hormonal phase approaching; HRAS/KRAS mosaicism).
**Counsel:** risk of secondary neoplasms in adult life, mostly benign (trichoblastoma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum); BCC rare (<1%). Watch for any new lump, ulcer or bleeding.

**Management:** refer routinely to paediatric dermatology. Observation or elective complete excision (narrow margin, timing shared with the family; earlier for the face). Biopsy any nodule. Look for syndromic features (Schimmelpenning) if the lesion is extensive.
**Differential course teaching raised:** linear morphoea *en coup de sabre* (acquired, indurated, progressive, which needs urgent treatment).

blocks.h: Case 3: 38-year-old man with a forehead nodule, punctum and odorous contents; 56-year-old woman with multiple painful lipomas

ul: **Diagnosis 1:** epidermoid (infundibular) cyst. **Syndrome association:** Gardner syndrome (FAP, APC): multiple early-onset cysts, osteomas, dental anomalies, desmoids, and colorectal polyposis.
**Management:** reassure. Treat inflammation without routine antibiotics. Elective complete excision of the cyst wall once quiet if criteria are met. Image midline dermoids first.

**Diagnosis 2:** Dercum's disease (adiposis dolorosa): painful lipomas, obesity, female, depression/fatigue. Symptomatic, multidisciplinary care; screen mood. Use NG12 sarcoma red flags for any enlarging lump.

ladder.t: Explain the pinch test and benign nature; shaving guard if it catches.

NHS **Evidence-Based Interventions**: only for diagnostic doubt, recurrent bleeding / infection, function or significant pain. Excision scar often bigger than the DF; recurrence if incomplete; cryo / shave leaves white mark (specialist / GP-surgeon decision).
Routine dermatology if uncertain or symptomatic; eruptive DFs on immunosuppressants: review drugs.

refer.t: Changing pigmented lesion with atypical dermoscopy: suspected cancer pathway.
Growing beyond 2–3 cm, irregular, nodular or on the trunk: **DFSP**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Growing beyond 2–3 cm, irregular, nodular or on the trunk: think **DFSP** and refer.
Changing pigmented lesion with atypical dermoscopy: refer on a **suspected cancer pathway** (NICE NG12).
Itch or catching on razors; ulceration (rare).
Persists indefinitely; may flatten over years.

pearls: Teach the patient the pinch test and explain that it is "a little knot of scar-like tissue". Shaving over it causes bleeding; a shaving guard helps.
Many eruptive DFs in someone on immunosuppressants (e.g. methotrexate, biologics) or with possible SLE/HIV: check the drug list and consider whether investigations are warranted (GP/specialist).

A **painful DF** that the patient wants removed is a worked case in the [skin surgery](condition:skin-surgery-preop) notes surgery case. See the [skin surgery](condition:skin-surgery-preop) notes for the anticoagulant, latex and local anaesthetic issues.
Five years of slow growth fits DF, but **"growth" is still a 7-point major feature (2 points)**. Document the dimple sign and size, and photograph with a ruler for comparison.
In skin of colour, do not dismiss acral or nail pigmentation as "ethnic". See the [melanoma](condition:melanoma) notes (acral melanoma) and Hutchinson's sign.
